This study addresses the challenge of minimizing the occurrence of suboptimal behavior in adaptive control methods. By integrating reward-biased maximum likelihood estimation, we develop an optimized algorithm that directly addresses this issue. Our research proposes an estimator update rule, grounded in the likelihood function, and evaluates its convergence through theoretical analysis and simulations. Additionally, we integrate the estimator into a damping control system to test its performance in real-time settings. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in maintaining stability and preventing suboptimal oscillations in a single-degree-of-freedom damper system. The presented approach is also applicable to a range of adaptive control systems. Moreover, its adaptability to various estimation methods positions it to be a valuable tool for designing optimal control strategies. Details of the implementation can be found in the accompanying supplementary material.

with a projected annual data output of 150-230 TB that must be processed 
within hard deadlines to meet physics requirements. To meet these demands, 
data reprocessing tasks are prioritized over timely analysis, a cycle often 
repeated until completion due to resource constraints. This cycle can be 
reduced by leveraging the power of data analysis communities through the 
development of the Analysis Innovation Knowledge Lab (AIKL), a cloud-based 
platform that utilizes containerized analysis workflows to be easily shared and 
scaled. This platform's early adoption by ATLAS analysis teams has shown promise, 
with analysis workflows successfully deployed on AWS and scalable to meet the 
demands of HLbend2 physics requirements. Future plans aim to expand AIKL's 
availability to the broader ATLAS analysis community and explore its feasibility 
for wider use across LHC experiments. This research was supported by the ATLAS 
GCP and funding from Fermilab's Center for Particle Physics. Results from the

The underlying assumption is that metaphorical abstraction offers a more versatile and expressive framework for conveying novel concepts. This initial study presents a computational model that builds on existing knowledge graphs and metaphoric mappings. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach in generating abstracted metaphors that preserve their semantic integrity. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of AI-assisted creative tools that enhance innovation and understanding across different creative fields. The current work is a foundational step towards achieving this goal by providing a more expressive and accurate medium for communicating creative concepts. Training neural networks on vast amounts of temporal data is a computationally demanding task. To address this issue, we've developed a novel approach called Skip-Sideways, which optimizes backpropagation by selectively reviewing and propagating gradients as the neural network processes streaming data. Leveraging a technique called sketching, Skip-Sideways significantly accelerates the learning process while minimizing memory usage. Specifically, for Convolutional Neural Networks processing video data, Skip-Sideways offers substantial memory and speedup advantages over existing methods, making it suitable for real-time learning applications. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we've employed Skip-Sideways to train a CNN for classifying action videos in the ActivityNet-V1 and ActivityNet-V2 datasets, outperforming comparable results achieved through batch-based learning approaches. Moreover, our findings indicate that Skip-Sideways can be seamlessly integrated with other techniques, enabling real-time learning from unbounded temporal data. A notable approach in imitation learning is DICE, which enhances imitation by
minimizing the difference between the distributions of expert and agent behaviors.
Although DICE's distributionally robust loss function is effective, it can lead to
excessive exploration. A more conservative variant, ValueDICE, addresses this
issue by prioritizing low-cost actions but can result in suboptimal policies.
ValueDICE falls short because it doesn't fully leverage expert behavior, often
resulting in agents that are too cautious. To address this limitation, we
introduce a new imitation learning method called SoftDICE. Our approach combines
the benefits of DICE's distributionally robust effect and ValueDICE's conservative
action selection strategy. SoftDICE achieves this by introducing a probabilistic
loss function that encourages agents to explore while keeping their action
similar to the expert's. Our method's efficiency is demonstrated through
experiments on various continuous control tasks in Atari and MuJoCo environments,
where SoftDICE outperforms DICE and ValueDICE in terms of average return. When
evaluated using a distributional robustness metric, our results show that
SoftDICE's robustness exceeds that of ValueDICE but slightly lags behind DICE. To
further validate our approach, we conduct ablation studies, which reveal that
SoftDICE's performance is largely due to its ability to explore effectively while
staying close to the expert behavior. Our implementation is available on
GitHub. Additionally, we identify a limitation in ValueDICE's sampling method and
propose a new sampling strategy that improves performance. Our results are
comparatively evaluated with existing approaches in imitation learning. The code

However, these models have limitations in handling the complex spatio-temporal relationships within multi-child interaction videos. To overcome this, a new deep learning model, known as GraphEMD, has been proposed. This model utilizes a graph convolutional network that learns the complex spatio-temporal relationships by constructing a dynamic graph from multi-person pose estimates. The graph convolutional network then applies a multi-scale attention mechanism to learn the complex spatio-temporal relationships at multiple temporal scales. A novel loss function, cycle consistency loss, has also been introduced to prevent the model from losing spatial information. To evaluate the effectiveness of the model, a new multi-child interaction dataset was collected and a comprehensive evaluation was conducted. The results demonstrate that GraphEMD outperforms state-of-the-art models in child activity recognition, achieving a high accuracy of 93.5% on the proposed dataset. Furthermore, a thorough analysis of the model's robustness to domain shift was conducted, showing that GraphEMD has a high level of robustness to domain shift. Our approach, GDF, is capable of pruning models without ground truth data by using the output of a target model as the pseudo-label, thus reducing training data requirements. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that GDF can achieve comparable pruning results to state-of-the-art methods, all without requiring ground truth data knowledge. Entity linking datasets are typically created through rule-based systems that rely on Wikipedia's information.  However, these datasets may not accurately represent the complexities of real-world text, which often includes unlinked mentions and missing Wikipedia entries. To address this limitation, we've developed WikiGUM, a novel dataset that's annotated using crowdsourcing techniques, offering a more comprehensive ground truth at the sentence level.  By comparing WikiGUM with existing datasets like WikiData100, WLE2005, and TAC2013, we found that our new dataset enables more advanced entity linking models to be trained.  Specifically, our dataset's contextual information significantly enhances the performance of these models, allowing them to outperform previous state-of-the-art systems.  Furthermore, our research reveals that our dataset's ability to represent diverse and nuanced entity linking decisions leads to better performance on out-of-domain text, which is an important consideration for entity linking systems.  By making this dataset publicly available, we aim to facilitate the development of new and more sophisticated entity linking systems.  Our dataset's code and annotations can be accessed through the following repository: https://github.com/wiki-gum-team/wiki-gum.  Additionally, two entity linking challenges are now available: the "Entity Linking at Scale" challenge, which aims to test the scalability of entity linking systems, and the "Entity Linking with Missing Knowledge" challenge, which evaluates the ability of these systems to handle missing knowledge.  These challenges are designed to drive the development of more robust and high-performing entity linking systems.  The WikiGUM entity linking challenges are now open for submission through the following website: https://www.ekkb.kth.se/Research/ResearchChallenges/wal2022/. The detection of continuous gravitational waves remains an elusive goal in astronomy, with no known sources having been identified so far.  However, theoretical predictions suggest that neutron star binaries could be promising sources of continuous gravitational waves due to their rapidly spinning nature, which could produce stable gravitational wave patterns.  In this paper, we present results from searches for continuous gravitational waves from neutron star binaries in our galaxy, specifically from systems with orbital periods of less than 200 days and neutron stars spinning at speeds of up to 1000 Hz.  Our analysis of data from the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Event Horizon Telescope Project, collected between 2015-2019, did not identify any gravitational wave signals that deviate significantly from predicted patterns, while setting new limits on the amplitude of such signals at various frequencies.  For example, we established upper limits on the amplitude of such signals from systems with spinning periods of 100-1000 Hz and orbital periods of 20-200 days at levels of $-15.3$ and $-19.4$ in units of nanohertz per hertz, at 90% confidence.  Our analysis also revealed a possible anomaly in the data from the observation run GO-1, which lasted from September 2015 to December 2015 and produced a signal with an amplitude of $-11.1$ in nanohertz per hertz at 95-100 Hz, although further investigation is needed to verify the authenticity of this finding.  Furthermore, we discuss the detection capabilities of our search procedure and the implications of these results for the study of neutron star binaries.  Our analysis also highlights the need for more advanced search algorithms that can accurately detect and characterize the patterns of continuous gravitational waves from these sources. Training deep neural networks with large datasets can be done in batches, 
typically using a single batch size. However, this approach has a significant 
drawback: it forces the model to learn from a fixed set of inputs, rather than 
averaging the performance across the entire dataset, resulting in a biased 
model that generalizes poorly. This problem is particularly pronounced when 
using stochastic gradient descent, standard data augmentation, and large batch 
training sizes. Our research proposes a new approach: aligning the data 
distributions within each mini-batch to address this issue. This method 
enables neural networks to learn more robust features, leading to improved 
performance on the test set. Our experiments show that this technique can be 
applied across different datasets and neural networks, regardless of their 
architecture. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that this technique can be 
used in conjunction with other methods, such as mixup and label smoothing, to 
further enhance performance. The code for our method can be found on the 
GitHub repository "batch alignment". 

We have also conducted experiments on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet 
datasets using various state-of-the-art models, including ResNet-34, Wide 
ResNet, and DenseNet. The results show that our Batch Alignment method achieves 
the state-of-the-art performance on the CIFAR datasets while being competitive on 
ImageNet. The method also demonstrates a significant improvement in the 
generalization of deep neural networks, even when using a large batch size. 

Our research also explores the theoretical underpinnings of batch alignment, 
proposing a new theory: the excess risk error bound. This error bound is a 
measure of the difference between the expected risk and the training loss. Our 
analysis reveals that aligning data distributions across mini-batches reduces 
this error bound, effectively minimizing the difference. The theoretical 
implications of our method are far-reaching and have significant implications 
for the field of deep learning. 

Finally, our work also investigates the potential for batch alignment to be 
applied to real-world problems, such as image classification and reinforcement 
learning, where it has shown promising results. The code for our method is freely 
available for use in these fields. The code can be found on the GitHub 
repository "batch alignment".

The goal of exact optimization is to create a precise solution with the least amount of effort possible. In the context of circuit optimization, this involves finding the smallest circuit that can output a specific binary pattern. Our research focuses on developing an efficient method to design a suitable circuit of a certain size 'n' to produce an output of '2^n' unique binary strings. Interestingly, we found that finding the smallest circuit is an NP-hard problem, which implies that as circuit size decreases, the difficulty of the problem increases. However, for larger circuits, our proposed greedy algorithm performs comparably with the best known approximation algorithm. In addition, we investigated finding the smallest circuit to produce all possible $2^n$ binary patterns, which we found to be an even harder problem, and developed an approximation algorithm that achieves a near-optimal circuit size. These findings contribute to the understanding of circuit optimization and open up possibilities for future research in related areas. The algorithms developed in this study can be adapted to tackle similar circuit optimization problems. Finally, we explored the possibility of using quantum algorithms to solve circuit optimization problems more efficiently than classical algorithms. Our analysis suggests that, in practice, quantum algorithms may not offer a significant advantage in circuit optimization. Despite the recent surge in interest, there has been a scarcity of research focused on developing innovative methods for information seeking within this complex environment. The rapid dissemination of COVID-19 via infectious disease has been paralleled by the swift spread of misinformation about the coronavirus through social media. Accurately identifying fake news has critical implications during the pandemic, making it necessary to develop sophisticated methods for news classification on social media. Traditional machine learning models, which rely on data features, often struggle with the complexity of news data. Conversely, deep learning models have shown remarkable success in processing large amounts of data, particularly images and videos. This paper proposes a cutting-edge deep learning framework that utilizes a transformer architecture to classify news content on social media. We evaluate the effectiveness of this framework using two datasets: COVID-19-Fake-COVID and COVID-19-Fake-COVID2. We compare the performance of the proposed model with existing deep learning techniques, achieving notable improvements in accuracy. Notably, the proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving accuracy rates of 96.19% and 96.65 % on the COVID-19-Fake-COVID and COVID-19-Fake-COVID2 datasets respectively. We introduce RAWMatch, a novel image matching pipeline that leverages RAW images. By processing RAW images, we can enhance image matching accuracy, particularly in low-light environments, by recovering detailed textures and color information that are lost in compressed JPEG images. Building upon this concept, we propose a practical image matching approach that efficiently handles RAW and JPEG images equally. The pipeline's versatility extends to various modalities, including video frames and point clouds, making it compatible with existing matching techniques. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RAWMatch, showcasing superior results in image registration, SLAM, and visual localization applications. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/feixk/RAWMatch.

This paper introduces a novel self-supervised learning framework, IPUI, tailored to mitigate the effects of class imbalance. IPUI leverages a pre-trained model to generate a diverse set of negative samples from its positive class, promoting robust positive class representations while refining the negative class representations through discriminative learning. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate IPUI's superiority over existing methods, achieving significant improvements in F1-score. Additionally, IPUI showcases exceptional adaptability and balance in handling datasets with varying degrees of imbalance. Deep Q-Networks, an essential component of deep reinforcement learning, have been widely utilized in various applications. However, the traditional Deep Q-Network algorithm, utilizing a multi-layer neural network to approximate the optimal Q-function, inherently suffers from overestimation issues, which often lead to suboptimal solutions. In an attempt to resolve this problem, we have developed a novel approach that utilizes a neural network with a tailored architecture. This new network structure incorporates weight distribution parameters that deviate from a standard Gaussian pattern. In our proposed algorithm, the optimal Q-function is approximated by leveraging a mixture of Gaussian distributions. This approach is implemented through a neural network with two distinct layers, each comprising a fixed number of output units that follow a Gaussian distribution. The weight parameters of these distributions are adjusted during training, and the optimal Q-function is calculated by summing the contributions of each individual Gaussian distribution. In doing so, the overestimation issue is effectively resolved, and the optimal solutions are achieved. In addition to theoretical analysis, the efficacy of our proposed algorithm is demonstrated through experiments on various reinforcement learning problems. Specifically, the algorithm is shown to outperform existing methods on the Cartpole and AirLift environments, achieving superior results in a remarkably short training time. Moreover, the algorithm successfully solves the classic Mountain Car problem, which has been a long-standing challenge for existing DQN variants. In summary, the proposed algorithm offers a straightforward yet effective solution to the overestimation problem plaguing traditional DQN algorithms. This new approach is expected to facilitate further advancements in deep reinforcement learning. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed voxel-based representations, which can be trained on modern graphics processing units (GPUs). Despite their efficiency, voxel-based models have inherent limitations, including high memory requirements and reduced precision. To address these challenges, a new approach has been proposed, combining the benefits of point-voxel representations and learning on GPUs while maintaining high precision. This approach involves initially sampling and refining point-voxel representations to optimize their structure and efficiency. The resulting representation is then used in a novel neural network architecture that employs a point-voxel fusion module to enhance accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this representation and associated network in 3D object detection tasks, showing improved precision and faster inference times compared to existing methods. This paper develops exact solutions for the time-dependent Mathieu equation, incorporating a position-dependent mass system within the context of a finite well potential. The derived solutions reveal periodic patterns in phase space, characterized by stable and unstable cycles. An examination of the underlying symmetry group associated with the equation yields a representation governed by the Lie algebra su(2). Furthermore, we investigate the effect of the position-dependent mass on the periodic trajectories, determining the critical value at which stability is lost. The relationship between the system's parameters is also investigated through phase space analysis. Specifically, we identify and analyze the distinct motion types exhibited by the system, including bounded, unbounded, and periodic motion. The results are supported by numerical simulations that demonstrate the system's behavior over time. The widespread dissemination of fake news via social media poses a significant threat to public discourse. We introduce a novel machine learning approach, termed the "learnability lock," 
which enables users to restrict models from accessing specific training data points.
This is achieved by training the model to predict outcomes for a subset of data 
and concealing the original data values. The learnability lock can be utilized in 
various contexts, such as limiting access to training examples containing sensitive 
information or preventing models from utilizing training data with known flaws. 
We assess the learnability lock's effectiveness and determine its practical 
application as an extension of regular training, requiring minimal additional 
effort and not compromising model performance, while providing additional benefits. 
Furthermore, we propose potential use cases and discuss potential risks and their 
feasible mitigation strategies. Lastly, we highlight potential future research 
directions and challenges associated with the learnability lock.

The identification of high-density materials is crucial for ensuring nuclear security due to its significance in non-proliferation, safeguards, and export control. To address this challenge, we developed a novel deep learning approach combining a deep convolutional neural network with a Siamese architecture. This method was trained using a large-scale dataset of 6 high-density material classes and 5 low-density material classes derived from the NIST International Molybdenum Disulfide dataset. The results indicate that our approach can effectively classify high-density material classes with 99.5% accuracy at the material category level and 97.5% accuracy at the material species level, even when dealing with a new, unseen material. This research demonstrates the practicality of deep learning in developing automated systems for detecting high-density materials in nuclear contexts, such as ports and inspection points. Deep learning-based systems are increasingly used for detecting fraudulent transactions due to their high accuracy and efficiency. However, adversarial attacks can compromise their performance by creating malicious inputs that the models incorrectly identify as legitimate. To counter these threats, our study proposes a new approach to creating adversarial examples and develops a defense mechanism to mitigate their effects. By analyzing the characteristics of the adversarial attacks and the underlying data, we employ a technique called Wasserstein distance to detect and prevent the attacks. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our method is effective against a range of adversarial attacks and outperforms existing approaches in detection accuracy. Specifically, our approach achieved a true detection rate of 99.5% for Fast Gradient Sign attacks, significantly improving upon previous methods that achieved true detection rates of 0.8% and 99.2%. These findings suggest that adversarial detection approaches can be optimized by leveraging distributional analysis and identifying the key differences between adversarial examples and legitimate inputs. Ultimately, our results have implications for the development of more robust deep learning models in the context of fraud detection. In this paper, we introduce a graph attention network to accelerate the mean-field inference algorithm for paired Conditional Random Fields by utilizing attention mechanisms and graph structures that naturally occur within paired data. The proposed network outperforms its neural network-based mean-field inference counterpart, achieving improved convergence on various tasks. The proposed network enhances the accuracy of the generalized mean-field algorithm while maintaining comparable efficiency, outperforming existing state-of-the-art results on the MNIST-m and MNIST-n-n datasets while achieving a 3-fold speedup. Notably, our method is the first to achieve high accuracy using mean-field inference on the MNIST-n-n dataset. We also demonstrate its effectiveness on the MNIST-m dataset and show that it can be integrated with other generalized mean-field approximations to achieve comparable accuracy at a lower computational cost. Experimental evaluations on diverse tracking scenarios demonstrate the superiority of the proposed active learning method in enhancing the performance of deep CNNs with a minimal number of labeled data. Compared to existing active learning strategies, the results show significant improvements, with the highest AUC scores across multiple datasets. Accurate crop production is crucial for reliable food security. The two key components of crop production are yield and quality. The latter, in particular, is vital for ensuring food safety, making it a priority to monitor quality along agricultural supply chains. The main challenge lies in collecting sufficient data to create a comprehensive quality assessment system. To overcome this obstacle, we developed a crop quality assessment method using hyperspectral remote sensing data. Our approach involves designing an attention-based convolutional neural network to analyze hyperspectral data and predict crop quality. The attention mechanism helps focus on the most significant spectral bands, significantly reducing the number of required spectral bands by 90%. Our method was tested on potato and wheat datasets, yielding superior results compared to previous methods. For potato, our model achieved an F1 score of 0.89 and for wheat, it reached an F1 score of 0.83. The findings indicate that hyperspectral remote sensing can be an effective tool for crop quality assessment. The developed algorithm and model are promising starting points for establishing a crop quality assessment system using hyperspectral remote sensing data. Moreover, we propose a framework for integrating hyperspectral remote sensing data into crop quality assessment systems. We investigate the behavior of the specific heat capacity and susceptibility in high-dimensional Ising systems under different boundary conditions. Through a mean-field analysis, we discover a significant difference in the scaling of susceptibility between systems with periodic and Neumann boundary conditions. This disparity stems from distinct sub-volume contributions, leading to different effective spatial dimensions. Consequently, our analysis predicts that the critical exponents associated with periodic boundary conditions match the Ising model's mean-field value, whereas those with Neumann boundary conditions behave like the three-dimensional Ising system. Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance in various tasks but struggle with distribution shifts, which occurs when the training and testing data have different distributions. Domain adaptation, a technique that utilizes a shared feature space for different domains, has been proposed to address this challenge. Domain adaptation is considered a more challenging problem than traditional supervised learning, as it requires the model to adapt to the testing domain's distribution. Despite its potential, successful domain adaptation remains an elusive goal. This paper aims to provide insights into the domain adaptation process by conducting a thorough analysis of the testing domain distribution using a dataset with labeled testing data. The results show that current domain adaptation methods fail to fully capture the underlying distribution shift, resulting in reduced performance. The study also highlights the limitations of using metrics like accuracy to assess domain adaptation models, as these metrics can be misleading when testing data is not available. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that using labeled testing data can significantly improve the performance of domain adaptation models. The findings of this study are expected to inform the development of more effective domain adaptation methods. In collaborative working environments, robots are becoming more prevalent.  In such settings, mobile robots are expected to safely navigate around people, yet often their navigation strategies simply compare sensor data to a set threshold to determine whether to stop, speed up, or change direction. This comparison-based approach can lead to overly cautious behavior and reduced efficiency, especially when encountering obstacles that vary in size. This paper introduces an empowerment-based navigation framework that enhances a robot's ability to operate efficiently and safely coexist with humans. This framework rewards the robot for developing a sense of control over the workspace, including detecting obstacles in its path, maintaining a safe distance, and keeping people at bay. We evaluate our framework in real-world settings, comparing it to a comparison-based baseline and demonstrating that it promotes more efficient navigation while ensuring human safety. Notably, empowered robots completed tasks 35% faster than their comparison-based counterparts and exhibited improved compliance with human-distance guidelines, suggesting that empowerment is a valuable strategy for developing robots capable of efficiently and effectively sharing workspaces with humans. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of human-robot collaboration and provides a foundation for creating more adaptable and efficient human-robot teamwork systems. This research introduces a method for resampling 3D point clouds that preserves their structure, using a hypergraph signal processing approach. The proposed technique starts by converting the point cloud into a hypergraph, then defines a spectral filter that can be applied to the graph signal to perform the resampling. Moreover, this technique allows for the creation of new, more detailed point cloud representations by selectively refining dense regions while simplifying sparse ones. Previous studies on grammatical error correction have focused primarily on developing systems that can learn from human corrections, but have not fully considered the differences in how humans perceive various error types. To bridge this gap, we conducted an initial study to understand how humans perceive the importance of distinct grammatical error types, specifically in the context of written English. Our analysis is based on a unique dataset comprising corrections provided by non-native English speakers, who rated error types on a scale of importance (1-5) and duration (1-5 minutes) in resolving them. The findings suggest that certain error types are perceived as easier to correct, such as punctuation errors, and more challenging when errors occur in the mid-sentence, rather than at the sentence boundary. We further explore how these human perceptions can be leveraged to develop more accurate and efficient grammar correctors. Additionally, we found that incorporating data from native speakers who are not experts in grammar correction can lead to improved performance in certain error correction tasks. The dataset and code used in our study is available for further research and exploration. The dataset can be found at https://github.com/anneman/GEC-Human-Perception. In online recommendation platforms, a standard approach displays a curated list of only the most appealing items. However, this limited presentation may conceal the quality of similar recommendations displayed elsewhere within the system. We investigated the quality of recommendations on the movie rental platform Netflix by analyzing user interactions and item features. Our findings reveal that the displayed ordered list significantly biases the top-ranked recommendations, directing users to less-preferred items. Furthermore, we discovered that showing the full item list, rather than just the top, results in a greater number of recommendations being accepted by users. To address this issue, we propose a simple strategy for enhancing recommendation quality, which can be easily applied to various online recommendation systems. Experimental results confirm that this approach is effective and easy to implement. Our research contributes a novel perspective on the quality of recommendations by analyzing the user's entire interaction with the system. The insights gained can help develop more effective recommendation systems that better serve users' needs. It is well established that repeated measurements speed up the quantum evolution of a system, but the underlying reason for this acceleration is still being researched. We examine a simple quantum model to better understand how this acceleration occurs, focusing on its behavior over time and how it is influenced by the type and frequency of measurements made. We compare this dynamic to a similar process in classical systems to gain a deeper insight into the quantum speed-up, attributing it to a balance between the preservation of a system's initial state and the level of information exposed through measurement, thereby affecting its rate of change. We also explore the implications of our findings on the nature of quantum mechanics and the relationship between information and change. Ultimately, while our analysis provides a partial explanation for the observed acceleration, a more comprehensive understanding will require further research into the fundamental principles governing the interplay between information, change, and the laws of physics. We introduce a novel technique called "Grainy" that enables the creation of lightweight neural networks without the need for iterative pruning. Grainy takes a conventional, fully-connected neural network and transforms it into a more efficient, sparse model by strategically replacing complex components with simpler ones that share similar parameters. This approach allows Grainy to achieve high sparsity levels of up to 95% while maintaining a comparable performance to the original model. Grainy's underlying mechanism is based on the principle of feature extraction, where the model learns to extract essential features from its inputs by discarding unnecessary information. As a result, the model size is reduced, and the computational complexity is minimized. Interestingly, Grainy's effectiveness is not affected by the model's size, and it can produce impressive results regardless of the network's complexity. Furthermore, Grainy can be applied to a wide range of machine learning models, including convolutional networks, and it can be used for tasks such as image classification, object detection, and more. In our experiments, Grainy consistently outperformed other pruning methods, including magnitude- and threshold-based approaches. Grainy's implementation is available on GitHub, and it can be easily integrated into various machine learning workflows. In conclusion, Grainy offers a straightforward and efficient method for creating compact neural networks, making it a valuable tool for machine learning researchers and practitioners. Its effectiveness can be demonstrated through a series of experiments, and it can be used for a range of machine learning applications, including image classification, object detection, and more. In the context of wave scattering, unbounded domains often pose difficulties when formulating conditions at infinity. To address this challenge, we develop a domain transformation method that maps an unbounded to a bounded domain, thereby simplifying scattering problems. This approach is initially demonstrated for time-harmonic elastic scattering problems, where an exact transformation is used to create a finite model. Subsequently, the transformation is extended to the time-domain, where it draws inspiration from the exact time-domain Green's function to design a numerical scheme for the time-reversal problem. To overcome computational difficulties, the scheme is reformulated in the frequency domain, where it is combined with a domain transformation method. This combined approach is numerically validated for a specific time-domain elastic scattering problem. Finally, the scheme is extended to the acoustic case and numerically tested for a specific time-domain acoustic scattering problem. Numerical results are provided to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. All simulations were performed using MATLAB. Federated learning's personalization challenge involves training unique machine learning models for each user. A collaborative approach called personalized federated learning over hypernetworks tackles this issue by training a high-dimensional model for each user. This method, however, faces a significant computational burden due to the high memory requirements. To resolve this problem, a new technique called FL-HNGD is introduced. It utilizes a more efficient training method based on gradient descent with data normalization, reducing the model size and associated memory costs by a factor of d, where d represents the model's dimension. Additionally, FL-HNGD offers a theoretical framework that demonstrates its ability to achieve the same optimal results as the original method while minimizing data transmission requirements. This enables users to locally update their models using only a small subset of the user's data, thereby reducing data transmission delays. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of FL-HNGD and its ability to achieve optimal results with reduced computational complexity. This method is also shown to be more efficient than existing techniques, such as federated averaging with data normalization, by a factor of d. Moreover, FL-HNGD is more robust to non-IID data and adversarial attacks than other methods, and it can achieve the same optimal results with fewer users. This method is also shown to be more efficient and robust than other techniques, such as personalized federated learning with data normalization, adversarial training, and model distillation. We present a gradient iterative approach for solving symmetric generalized eigenvalue problems, employing the gradient of the Schur complement matrix to achieve convergence. This enhanced iteration scheme is shown to outperform GMRES through numerical trials. In the medical field, gathering patient symptoms is crucial for accurate diagnosis.
However, current approaches focus on explicit symptoms, while neglecting implicit symptoms associated with patient conditions.
To bridge this gap, we present SymTag, a tag prediction model that utilizes pre-trained medical embeddings to identify implicit symptoms.
Our experimental analysis demonstrates the model's effectiveness in extracting implicit symptoms from unstructured text data. The findings indicate that SymTag outperforms established methods in terms of precision, particularly for more complex symptoms, while also improving the efficiency of training. Furthermore, we demonstrate SymTag's ability to enhance the performance of downstream tasks such as diagnosis systems. Notably, our results show that SymTag can be effectively integrated into existing systems, including DeepMedMind, to improve their overall performance. Recent advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs) have significantly impacted computer vision tasks such as image classification and image segmentation. However, it appears that GANs are not ideal for synthetic image generation in computer vision due to their reliance on self-supervised learning. In contrast, supervised image generation methods have shown more promise but are plagued by the issue of domain shift. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that combines self-supervised and supervised image generation techniques. Our method, which we term "self-supervised supervised image generation," enables the direct transfer of a self-supervised pre-trained model to downstream tasks without the need for fine-tuning. Our results, which are based on extensive experiments involving multiple datasets and architectures, demonstrate the efficacy of this approach and show that it can be applied to a wide range of image generation tasks with minimal adaptation required. Our findings suggest that self-supervised supervised image generation can be a powerful tool for computer vision tasks, and we hope this work will inspire further research in this area. The code and models used in our experiments will be publicly available upon acceptance. This approach can be applied to a wide range of image generation tasks, and we believe it has the potential to be applied to other computer vision tasks in a similar way. Recent advances in natural language processing have significantly improved the efficiency of language models.  However, these models are vulnerable to errors caused by hardware malfunctions such as broken neurons.  To mitigate this issue, we developed a new learning technique called Multitask Mask Mixture Pretraining (M3P) that trains language models to perform multiple tasks simultaneously.  Our research shows that this approach improves a model's resilience to errors significantly outperforming existing methods.  To validate our technique, we created MixUP-NLP, a benchmark for testing language model robustness and applied it to various pretraining methods.  Our analysis found that MixUP-NLP is more effective at enhancing robustness than traditional methods, especially when combined with multitask learning.  Moreover, we discovered that a model's ability to perform well across different tasks is closely linked to its overall robustness.  Our research offers a new approach for training robust large language models for various applications.  The MixUP-NLP benchmark and pretraining code are now available for public use.  Our work is expected to inspire further innovation in the development of robust language models.  The code can be accessed at https://github.com/NLPatUT/MixUP-NLP. classified against a list of specific medical conditions. A deep learning model is
trained to distinguish between healthy and unhealthy frames, with the goal of accurately
identifying the medical condition causing the abnormal speech. To evaluate the
proposed approach, a dataset of speech recordings from patients with respiratory
insufficiency was collected and compared to a control group of healthy individuals.

In the active learning framework, we examine a novel setting where a learner is tasked with identifying the best subset of data points to query from an initial, unlabeled dataset. The corresponding labels in the query dataset are then utilized to fine-tune a task model, which is subsequently employed to predict labels for the remaining, unlabeled data points. We propose an algorithm that aims to minimize the total error in the prediction of the unlabeled data points, leveraging the task model. The algorithm is based on a two-stage optimization process, where the learner first selects an optimal subset of data points from the unlabeled dataset, and then refines the task model using the chosen data points. The selection of data points is achieved by minimizing a specific objective function, which is derived from the gradient descent process of the task model's parameters. The algorithm is further enhanced by incorporating a regularization term that helps to prevent overfitting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through its superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets, compared to existing state-of-the-art active learning methods. The proposed algorithm is also computationally efficient, with a worst-case time complexity of O(k^2 * d * ln N), where k is the number of data points to be queried, d is the dimensionality of the data points, and N is the total number of data points in the unlabeled dataset. We have conducted a detailed analysis of the specific angular momentum within a disk that surrounds a protostar, utilizing data from the Bok's object star formation simulation. We discovered that within a specific radius of approximately 290 au, the specific angular momentum exhibits a notable increase. This can be attributed to the transfer of angular momentum from surrounding material, such as in the case of accretion and migration. Consequently, the angular momentum within this range deviates significantly from its expected theoretical value, amounting to approximately 30% less than predicted. Moving further outwards, beyond the radius of 290 au, the specific angular momentum demonstrates a stable pattern that aligns closely with its expected theoretical value, suggesting that the outer disk maintains solid rotation. This finding is consistent with previous research on star-forming disks, specifically those related to Class 0 and I protostars. Additionally, our study highlights the significant role played by accretion in determining the specific angular momentum within star-forming disks. This finding is further supported by the inclusion of a disk accretion model, which helps to explain the observed patterns in specific angular momentum within the simulated disk. Finally, we also found that the simulated disk exhibits a notable degree of flaring, with the midplane density profile increasing at a rate of approximately 1.6 times the expected rate, suggesting that the disk may be subject to external influences, such as in the case of a disk that is being perturbed by the movement of a planet. This finding is consistent with previous research on star-forming disks, specifically those related to Class 0 and I protostars. The results of this study are expected to provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of disks that surround protostars. This research examines the feasibility of using single-subframe allocation in Cellular-V2V networks to reduce control and synchronization message delays. We introduce an innovative scheduling strategy that distributes available resources to multiple vehicles within a subframe, ensuring each vehicle receives a dedicated resource when needed. We analyze the effects of this approach on packet delay, accounting for both uplink and downlink transmissions, traffic patterns, and scheduling algorithms. The results reveal that single-subframe allocation can significantly minimize delays, particularly when compared to the current subframe-splitting method. Notably, this method has the potential to achieve a maximum delay reduction of nearly 50% even with existing scheduling algorithms and a significant improvement of up to 90% under optimal conditions. Additionally, our study shows that increasing the number of available resources can further enhance scheduling performance. A key takeaway from this study is that future Cellular-V2V systems should prioritize streamlining resource management processes, including the implementation of more efficient scheduling algorithms. Multilevel algorithms, specifically algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods, are renowned for efficiently solving vast linear equations derived from continuous and finite difference problems. Yet, their widespread adoption is restricted due to the intricacies of their algorithmic design and implementation, making them inaccessible to many researchers. To mitigate this challenge, a comprehensive, open-source library called Automg has been developed to provide a stable and adaptable AMG framework. This library boasts a user-friendly interface, allowing users to leverage various AMG configurations through a single function call. Furthermore, it offers advanced features, such as automated selection of the V- or Q-cycling approach, full support for parallelization, and specialized procedures for handling complex block matrices. To facilitate seamless integration, the library includes tools for compatibility with the Eigen and MPI frameworks. This report delves into the core principles behind Automg, including its implementation within the Eigen framework, through a detailed, step-by-step explanation. Moreover, a range of relevant examples are presented to demonstrate the library's capabilities and provide a foundation for future contributions. In many classification tasks, training a sophisticated neural network from scratch can be impractical due to limited available data. Transfer learning offers a solution by allowing the model to leverage knowledge from a related task, often in the form of pre-trained models. This approach is particularly beneficial when combined with fine-tuning, which involves adjusting the model's parameters to suit the new task. While fine-tuning is typically applied to the model's final layer, our research explores a more extreme version of transfer learning known as extreme fine-tuning, where more parameters are adjusted than in traditional methods. We compared the effectiveness of fine-tuning and extreme fine-tuning in scenarios with limited available data and found that extreme fine-tuning consistently outperformed fine-tuning. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that extreme fine-tuning can yield better results than training a model from scratch, even when sufficient data is available. Researchers have successfully applied SNNs to various tasks, including visual recognition, reinforcement learning, and more, primarily in binary mode. However, current SNN models are limited by their binary output nature, which hinders their performance on multi-class classification tasks. Utilizing this relationship allows us to derive a novel $O(a^2)$ subleading correction to the pseudoscalar mass, effectively reducing the original $O(a\mu)$ term associated with quark mass disparities in the Schroedinger functional approach. Additionally, our results are in close agreement with Nf=2 staggered quark mass estimates obtained from the HPQCD Collaboration. This alignment further supports our use of the axially-variant method in calculating quark masses. The calving front's variability has a substantial impact on glacier systems, influencing calving, ice flux, and ocean forcing. A statistical model is presented that accounts for this variability in the context of glacier-ocean interactions, using the Little Ice Age (LIA) glacier as a case study. The model's parameters are adjusted to match observed conditions during the LIA period and early 20th-century era, showing that a fluctuating ocean forcing can significantly impact glacier states. Specifically, the parameters suggest that ocean forcing variations can cause up to a 100m change in glacier height and ice flux, and can also delay a glacier's retreat by up to 50 years. These findings are consistent with observations of the Serac Glacier, providing strong evidence for the importance of calving front fluctuations in glacier dynamics. Ultimately, the statistical model offers a valuable tool for reconstructing past glacier fluctuations and predicting future ice flux, especially in scenarios where ocean forcing is expected to change. By analyzing historical glacier fluctuations in conjunction with ocean forcing patterns, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between glaciers and their surroundings. A future statistical model is also proposed to integrate glacier and ocean dynamics, providing a more comprehensive view of glacier-ocean interactions. The results of this study will inform future glacier modeling efforts and provide valuable insights into the behavior of glaciers in response to ocean forcing. Integrating entities into neural generation models is crucial for maintaining coherent and accurate information in generated text. Despite the importance of entity information, its incorporation into these models has been limited due to the high computational demands of sophisticated entity encoders. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing entity-based generative models, producing text that is both accurate and grammatically correct. Furthermore, our method exhibits improved performance compared to a standard neural generation model that does not utilize pre-trained entity embeddings. In this research, we investigate how sudden currency fluctuations affect global online labor markets. We analyze devaluations' impact on real wages of workers from devaluing countries in a global setting where labor markets connect with spot currency markets through crowdsourcing platforms that act as intermediaries. These platforms determine workers' wages in US-drawn transactions, converting their local currency earnings into US dollars. Our findings show that sharp currency fluctuations result in significant real wage losses for workers from devaluing countries resulting from their local currency's depreciation. To mitigate this loss, platform owners can shift work to other countries with stronger currencies, known as cross-border crowdyard shifting. However, this adjustment may cause real wages to change in the shifting country as well. We present a mechanism that allows platform owners to make an optimal decision on work redistribution across countries, taking into account the dynamic effects of their actions. Our results show that platform owners can design a mechanism that makes everyone better off, even in cases where some countries experience losses. This research has implications for the global labor market and the devaluation effects that occur within it. It also explores ways for platform owners to create mutually beneficial incentives for their workers and the spot markets they interact with. Our findings are relevant to the context of the gig economy, especially in the wake of the 2021 devaluation in Argentina, which led to real GDP drops of 6.9% and 7.7% in the US and Argentina respectively. The devaluation resulted in a 14.5% real wage drop in Argentina, prompting many US-based workers to shift work to other countries, resulting in a 4.6% real wage drop in the shifting countries. Our proposed mechanism can be used to design a mechanism that makes all parties better off in such scenarios. It can also be applied to other contexts, such as the ongoing effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on global markets. Our research has implications for the ongoing discussions on devaluation, labor market regulation, and gig economy reform. We also discuss the potential applications of our research in the context of blockchain and distributed ledger technology (DLT). Our research can be used to design a mechanism that makes all parties better off in various scenarios. We present a mechanism that can be used to create mutually beneficial incentives for platform owners and their users. We also discuss the potential applications of our research in the context of DLT, including the use of DLT to create a dynamic, blockchain-based labor market that can be used to create mutually beneficial incentives for platform owners and their users.

The main goal of high-performance parallelization involves not only correctly
translating sequential programs into parallel ones but also identifying the most
optimal execution configuration to maximize performance.
Existing parallelization techniques often face issues related to incorrect or
insufficient parallelism extraction, poor resource utilization, and the resulting
inefficiencies. To tackle these challenges, we propose an approach that utilizes
program semantics to guide the parallelization process, enabling the consideration
of hardware constraints and improving termination and convergence properties. This
approach is integrated into our Denovo system, which is based on operational
semantics and can recompile standard sequential programs written in standard
languages into parallel code with a global view. Specifically, we introduce a
framework for parallelizing programs written in standard languages for systems
with a graph-similarity model, which is capable of handling a wide range of graph
processing applications. We further enhance our parallelization framework with
a comprehensive optimization phase, which includes techniques for load balancing,
avoiding synchronization issues, and other performance-enhancing strategies. This
approach is demonstrated through the successful parallelization of key graph
processing applications, including PageRank, Graph-500, and Breadth-First Search. 
Our evaluation reveals significant speedup and efficiency in the execution of these
applications compared to their optimized parallel implementations. Notably, we
achieve a 3.12x average speedup over the sequential PageRank implementation and a
4.88x average speedup over the Graph-500 benchmark when compared to optimized parallel
implementations. Moreover, our optimization techniques demonstrate up to a
2.5x speedup over the optimized parallel code. This research is part of the NSF-CCF
grant No. CCF-1705933 and is further supported by the NSF-IEAP grant No.
IR-1626126. Additional details regarding this research, including a video, can be
found at https://research.google.com/pubs-archive/parallel-semantics.html. At the time of submission, the research is still ongoing and under development. A preliminary version of the related paper "Denovo: A Denotational Framework for the High-Performance Parallelization of Graph-Processing Applications" has been published in PPoRR 2021. The current paper extends upon this research, offering a comprehensive description of the entire parallelization process and providing further insights into the optimization techniques employed. Model-predictive control (MPC) is an effective method for managing intricate systems, yet its effectiveness heavily relies on the accuracy of the predictive model and the constraints. In scenarios where models are complex or uncertain, a more robust approach is necessary. To address this issue, a novel MPC strategy is proposed that utilizes a neural ordinary differential equation (NOE) to forecast the system's behavior. This NOE is updated at each control cycle and optimizes for a suitable performance metric. To enhance the strategy's robustness, a constraint is incorporated limiting the distance between consecutive NOE states. To mitigate the associated computational complexity, a novel sparse neural network architecture is developed. This new MPC method is demonstrated to be highly effective in managing challenging systems, such as a non-linear pendulum and a simulated Mini-Z magnetically levitated in mid-air. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis is provided to elucidate the strategy's key design elements and their respective trade-offs. This work is a pioneering achievement in the application of neural ordinary differential equations in model-predictive control scenarios. In the context of continuum-armed bandit problems, agents interact with a set of unexplored continuous options. The goal is to balance exploration and optimization to achieve the highest possible reward. In this research, we examine a scenario where the available options are arranged in a specific and limited manner - they form a single dimension with a defined order. This setup is common in real-world applications, such as recommending items to users. We have developed a new algorithm, Monotonous Continuum Multi-Armed Bandit (MC-MAB), which leverages the inherent order of the options to enhance its performance. In particular, MC-MAB exploits the options' monotonic nature to refine its estimates of each option's value, leading to improved exploration outcomes. Notably, MC-MAB can achieve a time complexity of O(n log n) and results in a regret O(n log n), representing the worst possible outcome. The algorithm's performance is demonstrated through experiments on both artificially generated and real-world datasets. The findings show that MC-MAB significantly surpasses existing continuum-armed bandit algorithms in terms of regret and the number of interactions required. The algorithm's advantages are particularly pronounced when dealing with options that exhibit a clear and limited order. When applied to options that lack a clear order, MC-MAB achieves comparable performance to existing state-of-the-art methods. This new format offers the potential to significantly simplify the sharing and comparison of innovative solutions within the deep learning community. This paper investigates distributed resource allocation within a multi-agent system, with the goal of maximizing individual utility. Building upon this framework, a dynamic approach is introduced, allowing agents to adapt their consumption rates in real-time, subject to utility gain constraints. This adaptation mechanism is achieved through a control law that regulates consumption rates and ensures stability. The efficacy of the proposed algorithms is substantiated through numerical examples, which demonstrate their ability to reach an optimal Nash equilibrium in a resource allocation game. Furthermore, the dynamic adaptation of consumption rates enables the system to respond to changing environments and demands. Notably, the numerical results show that the proposed dynamic algorithm converges faster than the non-adaptive version, achieving a superior solution within a shorter timeframe. Moreover, the utility gain under the adaptive algorithm exceeds that of the non-adaptive framework. All simulations were conducted using MATLAB software. The Integrated Sachs-Wolfe effect is a key factor in obtaining unbiased measurements of the integrated matter density across the universe, making it an essential tool in cosmological research. However, the ISW signal is relatively weak and can be easily distorted by other effects such as lensing and foreground contamination. To address these challenges, we have developed a novel approach that combines cross-correlation with temperature fluctuations and sophisticated foreground removal techniques using the Planck dataset. Our analysis reveals that cross-correlation between ISW and lensing induces a correlated noise signal that can be approximated by a band-limited power-law process. We have incorporated this noise signal into our ISW power spectrum analysis and demonstrated that it can be accurately estimated using the Planck temperature data. Furthermore, we have shown that our improved foreground removal technique significantly enhances the ISW signal, ultimately yielding a more precise measurement of the integrated matter density across the universe. Our analysis also reveals a significant improvement in the ISW power spectrum measurements, resulting in a 2.5σ discrepancy with the ΛCDM model predictions. These findings highlight the potential of the ISW effect in providing valuable insights into the integrated matter density and the properties of the universe. Few-shot learning involves learning new tasks using minimal labeled data, requiring existing knowledge from related tasks.  The main challenge is efficiently utilizing a limited number of examples, typically seven or fewer per class, for each new task.  To address this, we propose a novel framework called Meta-Emotion Transformer, specifically designed for meta-learning of emotional data.  The proposed framework leverages the advantages of meta-learning and self-supervised learning to enhance the generalizability of its components.  The Meta-Emotion Transformer is a hierarchical model that integrates a transformer to capture contextual information and a self-attention mechanism to capture emotional cues.  The model is initially fine-tuned on a variety of emotional datasets and then tested on new datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness.  Experimental results show that this approach achieves superior performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods in few-shot emotion recognition.  The proposed method significantly outperforms other methods, with notable improvements of 6.73%, 4.45%, and 2.42% in accuracy, uncalved, and unbalanced scenarios, respectively, when tested on the new datasets.  The code for this method will be publicly available after publication.  We also present a new dataset called EMO-DS for testing emotional language recognition and provide the corresponding code for its annotation process. A primary objective of dialog systems is to deduce user goals through classification based on the intent.  This classification process is a challenging task, particularly in languages lacking sufficient training data.  To address this issue, a new approach to intent classification has been developed using a combination of transfer learning and self-supervised learning.  This method utilizes a pre-trained language model, such as RoBERTa, and fine-tunes it using a limited set of labeled data in the target language.  Additionally, a self-supervised task is implemented by replacing dialog segments with corresponding intent labels, enabling the model to learn intent representations from unlabeled data.  This multi-task learning setup enhances the model's intent classification performance, particularly in scenarios with limited labeled data.  Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, particularly in Italian, a language lacking sufficient training data.  This method can be applied to any language where a suitable model exists and target dialog data are available.  Code and models are made available for public use. This paper focuses on weak amenability in Banach algebras, introducing its associated homology, Charlier derivatives, and Charlier differentials. We establish key findings, including the relationship between weak amenability and certain algebra properties, the characteristics of Charlier derivatives and differentials, and the conditions under which these notions exist. Additionally, our analysis reveals that certain Banach algebra properties are linked to the vanishing of specific homology groups. Specifically, a Banach algebra is weakly amenable if and only if its unitization's homology groups at degree one vanish. This implies that weak amenability can be determined by examining either Charlier derivatives or Charlier differentials, along with the first homology group of the unitization. This study employed advanced computational methods to analyze the magnetic properties of BaAlH10 in its ground state, as well as above its freezing point, utilizing first-principle calculations. This allowed us to determine the material's magnetic response to an external magnetic field across various temperatures. Notably, the results indicate that BaAlH10 exhibits anomalous diamagnetism at low temperatures, a phenomenon attributed to the intricate electronic structure of the material. This anomalous behavior is linked to the unique arrangement of Ba and H atoms, as well as the electronic states at the Fermi level, specifically the presence of flat bands. This unified approach is demonstrated using a range of test cases, including a single cell, a pair of cells, and a multicellular system, to validate its accuracy and efficiency. To further demonstrate its potential, a multicellular system is used to study the behavior of cancer cells in different environments, showing that the model can be used to study the behavior of complex biological systems. This integrated approach has the potential to provide a more realistic and comprehensive understanding of complex biological systems, by allowing for the simulation of cell behavior at a microscopic level while capturing the large-scale dynamics of the system. A pressing research issue in robotics is enabling robots to navigate through soft or deformable terrain. Generative adversarial models, such as Wasserstein GANs with Gradient Penalty (WGAN-GP), have achieved success in approximating optimal transport problems. These models can replicate the optimal coupling for which the Wasserstein distance is minimized. However, they often struggle to find the optimal coupling for cyclic OT problems. This is because enforcing non-negativity constraints on cyclic OT plans is difficult for WGAN-GP to satisfy. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach that incorporates cycle regularization into WGAN-GP to find the optimal cyclic plan that minimizes the Wasserstein distance. Our method, called Cyclic Wasserstein GAN with Gradient Penalty (CWGAN-GP), has been demonstrated to efficiently solve cyclic OT problems and simulate various real-world scenarios. For example, CWGAN-GP can be utilized to model the spread of diseases across populations by simulating the stochastic movement of individuals. Additionally, the model can be used to approximate the optimal transport cost of evolving systems, such as the movement of particles in a fluid. The results indicate that CWGAN-GP outperforms traditional methods in solving cyclic OT problems. Moreover, the model's ability to handle the non-negativity constraints of cyclic plans makes it well-suited for solving complex problems involving stochastic movement. The number of sunspots is widely regarded as a reliable gauge of solar activity.  However, due to the inherent variability and limitations in the data collection process, deriving precise numerical values can be challenging.  The number of sunspots is often calculated by either manually counting individual features or using automated algorithms that can be prone to errors.  In this study, a novel approach is presented for automatically identifying sunspot features within images of solar activity.  The method leverages the power of computer vision, specifically deep neural networks, to analyze the images and pinpoint the sunspots.  The performance of this technique is evaluated against human annotations on a large dataset of solar images and found to be remarkably effective, with an accuracy of over 96%. This research introduces a novel method for creating spatial patterns using Reinforcement Learning and Deep Convolutional Neural Networks. The approach focuses on training an agent to generate any desired spatial arrangement by guiding it through the optimal sequence of convolutional operations. The resulting patterns can be used to reconstruct the original input or serve as novel generative models in their own right. The developed algorithm is applied to the generation of both binary and continuous grain structures at the atomic scale, along with the creation of periodic patterns in higher dimensions. The findings of this study demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methodology, which is available as open-source software for the public to utilize. This note focuses on applying the Lyapunov condition to Markov chains in a discrete state space. It introduces a new Lyapunov condition, specifically designed for chains with jumps, and demonstrates its application in deriving drift and diffusion estimates for jump chains. This allows for the proof of a new criterion for which the drift is less significant compared to the diffusion, and it is this criterion that is central to the note. By leveraging this criterion, we establish a condition that ensures the drift term's impact on convergence is negligible, thereby facilitating the derivation of exponential convergence rates under minimal conditions. This represents an advancement over existing research in the field, such as [2,3,4], and our approach is distinguished by its broader applicability and weaker assumptions. Moreover, our findings can be applied to various scenarios, including chains with jumps, to provide new insights and improve upon existing results. To support our theory, we include several illustrative examples. This note is a revised and expanded version of [1], published in 2018 as an arXiv preprint. A significant portion of the results presented here are original contributions of the author, while a few additional results are adaptations of existing work. Specifically, our analysis of the Brownian and Levy-diffusion examples is based on [5] and further develops these ideas, whereas the examples related to the multinomial and general chains are entirely new and specifically focus on their jump dynamics. A related paper, titled "Jump process versions of Z2-entropy and Z2-action functionals", has been accepted for publication in the Electronic Journal of Probability. We establish a priori bounds for a class of nonlinear solids with a strain-limiting property, applicable to both quasi-static and dynamic scenarios. These bounds are derived using a method based on the Coleman-Ninomiya lemma, specifically tailored for dynamic systems with p-growth constraints on constitutive relations. A key consideration is ensuring that the strain-limiting condition is compatible with the chosen bounds, achievable by carefully choosing the value of p, which dictates the nonlinear behavior. For quasi-static applications, we demonstrate that a p-value of 2 is sufficient to yield independent bounds from the strain limit. In the context of dynamic systems, we show that a p-value of 2 is necessary and sufficient to prevent excessive nonlinear energy, allowing for more accurate bounds when assuming p equals 2. These findings are exemplified through applications to hyperelastic and Kelvin-Voigt materials. This research offers a practical approach to computing bounds for nonlinear solids, facilitating the efficient computation of approximations with a p-value of 2. The use of physics-informed neural networks in solving complex ordinary differential equations has gained significant attention recently. Despite their ability to accurately represent underlying physics, these networks often fail to converge due to the presence of multiple solutions or the presence of noise in data. This study proposes a novel approach that integrates neural networks with a continuation method, specifically the shooting method, to effectively solve a specific class of ordinary differential equations. The proposed approach has been successfully applied to the Black-Scholes equation, one of the most complex equations in finance, under varying conditions and model parameters, including those with extreme volatility. The results demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of this approach compared to the conventional shooting method and physics-informed neural networks. Additionally, this study reveals the limitations of the latter two methods and highlights the advantages of the proposed continuation method. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the proposed approach can be adapted to handle more complex equations and model scenarios, such as those with multiple dimensions, non-linear boundary conditions, and noisy data. The proposed approach has the potential to be extended to a broader class of ordinary differential equations. Current video conferencing systems struggle with poor network conditions, specifically when the connection is lost or severely delayed. Existing video codecs can handle some level of packet loss, but traditional methods, like linear prediction in H.263 and H.264, are insufficient under extreme degradation. As a result, many frames are discarded, including those with already completed encoding processes. To mitigate this issue, we've developed an innovative approach that allows incomplete encoded frames to contribute to decoded videos. This technique has been successfully integrated into the encoder and decoder of the H.263.2 video conferencing standard and has demonstrated notable performance enhancements under various loss patterns. In contrast to the original H.263.2 standard, our method exhibits significant improvements, increasing the maximum acceptable packet loss rate from 5% to 40% for low-bitrate settings and from 50% to almost total packet loss with minimal degradation in visual quality. This breakthrough paves the way for future research into further enhancing encoder design and the creation of more efficient error-resilient video codecs. The corresponding code and experimental results are publicly available for others to build upon. This research has been accepted for publication in the journal "IEEE Transactions on Communications". This process is contingent on the torque cycle's frequency and amplitude. By analyzing the effective energy landscape derived from this model, we have identified the role of the spin anchor site and optical active site in the material's response to the torque cycle. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the switching of magnetic moments occurs through the process of Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert precession, which is driven by the torque cycle. This process is analogous to a thermally assisted magnetic switching mechanism, which is facilitated by the energy barrier that is lowered by the torque cycle. Notably, we have found that the effective energy landscape exhibits a unique "V" shape, which is different from the previously reported "U" shape, and this shape is sensitive to the amplitude of the torque cycle. Moreover, we have demonstrated that the magnetic moments exhibit a non-reciprocal switching behavior, which is influenced by the frequency of the torque cycle. This finding provides a new understanding of the all-optical magnetic switching phenomenon in ferrimagnets, which is crucial for the development of high-density magnetic memory devices. Ultimately, our work contributes to the development of a new paradigm for the manipulation of magnetic moments in ferrimagnets using light. Our research introduces ARISE, a novel framework for the manipulation of garments using manipulation graphs. This approach creates an interface for articulating complex actions on clothing, breaking them down into manageable, graph-based tasks. To facilitate the use of existing articulation methods, we develop a standardized method for aligning key features such as articulation points, folds, and seams. This is further integrated with a garment recognition system to enable the identification of clothing types and their respective folds. The resulting system is capable of generating a wide variety of manipulation sequences for any type of clothing, including those without prior articulation information. To demonstrate the effectiveness of ARISE, we present a comprehensive set of experiments that include the identification of key features, the manipulation of clothing in 3D environments, and the ability to express complex actions in an intuitive graph-based interface. This approach allows the neural networks to be retrained with data from a single observation, and they can be shown to be effective in identifying genuine signals in real-time.
