Preparing comprehensive datasets for languages with limited available data poses significant challenges, primarily due to the extensive manual effort required to annotate and curate data. Traditional approaches to scaling dataset development are often restricted to augmenting existing data or leveraging related but unconnected data. We introduce an innovative inductive approach that enables the creation of new data by leveraging existing data and adapting to emerging patterns in the target domain. This method is demonstrated through the expansion of a existing dataset for the low-resource language Sindhi, which has been widely used in previous research. We utilize Sindhi text from various sources, including Wikipedia and news articles, to develop a robust model that can effectively categorize unseen Sindhi text from sources outside of our control. Unlike previous methods, which rely on annotated data, our approach eliminates the need for manual data annotation. We evaluate the performance of our model on classification tasks and demonstrate its ability to generalize and adapt to new data while maintaining high accuracy. The development of our inductive model marks a crucial step towards establishing a sustainable framework for dataset growth in low-resource languages. The design of this system involves a dynamic game among the agents, where each agent aims to minimize its own cost while considering the uncertainty of the others' actions. The optimal strategy involves each agent to create a predictive model of the other agents' actions and use it to make an informed decision. The outcome of this system is analyzed under different levels of cooperation and information availability. The key findings show that the system's performance improves significantly when all agents share information and cooperate. Furthermore, achieving perfect confidentiality of the state information is impossible, but it can be closely approximated by introducing minor disturbances. The study also reveals that the agents' performance can be optimized in the absence of information sharing if only local information is considered. To address this limitation, we propose a decentralized learning mechanism that enables agents to achieve the optimal performance level even in the absence of information sharing. This mode leads to a non-uniform exchange of spin between the two parts of the system. This process is facilitated by the fact that the antiferromagnetic particle's response to the oscillating vortex is highly dependent on its orientation relative to the vortex's center. Bilevel optimization problems involve hierarchical constraints that are unique in requiring the optimization of multiple objective functions within an upper and lower constraint framework. Most existing methods rely on first-order optimization techniques for the lower-level constraints. However, our work presents a novel approach that leverages second-order derivative information to improve the efficiency of these constraints. This is achieved by formulating an auxiliary problem that incorporates the Hessian of the lower-level functions and using it to obtain second-order information at the initial stage. We then utilize this information to derive a quadratic surrogate function for each lower-level problem and solve the bilevel problem through a proposed block descent strategy. Additionally, our approach allows for the optimization of problem-specific parameters and we evaluate their influence on the problem's convergence behavior. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate the effectiveness of our method compared to existing first-order based approaches. In open set recognition, a machine learning task, a model must identify whether an input belongs to a known class or not. We explore the connection between open set recognition and generative models, specifically the task of training a generative model that can not only produce samples from known classes but also accommodate novel classes with unknown characteristics. We examine the relationship between this generative model and a classifier capable of open set recognition. We propose a novel approach, based on a generative adversarial framework, to optimize the classifier's open set recognition performance by training it to generate samples from known classes and to distinguish between these classes and unknown novel ones. We also introduce a metric, the open set threshold, to evaluate and compare the performance of different models in this domain. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing models in achieving better classifier generalization and open set detection. Furthermore, our approach can be easily integrated into existing neural networks to serve as a plug-and-play solution for open set recognition tasks. We also provide a detailed analysis of our experimental results in the supplementary material. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the connection between generative models and open set recognition, paving the way for the development of more advanced models capable of handling out-of-distribution data in a variety of applications. We also explore the potential applications of our proposed method in other areas such as anomaly detection and semi-supervised learning. The implications of our findings are significant as they have the potential to improve the robustness and adaptability of machine learning models in a wide range of tasks. SVAR models face significant challenges in modeling high-dimensional time series data, 
particularly when dealing with a large number of cointegrating relationships. To address 
this issue, we incorporate the LASSO penalty into SVAR priors, allowing for strong 
shrinkage of parameters. Our method is applied in the context of the US economy, 
using data from the Great Recession. The results show that our proposed approach can 
identify structural shocks that are not visible in the conventional approach, 
considering correlations among structural VAR coefficients. The identified shocks 
distinguish the effects of the recession and financial crisis, providing valuable 
insights into the US economic cycle. The proposed LASSO-SVAR method is available in 
the rEMMGroup package on the GitHub platform.
